content: Welcome back to another YouTube video! I'm excited today to discuss a topic that's been catching on a little bit more lately, partially because I think I've been implementing it more and talking about it more. Two, it's kind of got coined as a name. The lifter I'm actually going to talk about in the case study today is Vaskar Carpio, one of my athletes, who has kind of coined this implementation of singles as fatigue singles. So, without further ado, today I want to get into how to program fatigue singles. So, what is a fatigue single? It's basically doing a single after your top rep set, instead of doing the single first. And that's not revolutionary; I didn't make this up. This isn't my principle that all of a sudden I originated. Honestly, I've been doing this for a long time, and someone did it before me, and someone did it before them. It's absolutely nothing new. But the reason I want to make this video is that what I think is new is my reasoning and how I program these over the macro cycle versus just looking at them as a simple tool. In other words, it's something I used to do occasionally, but now it's become more ingrained as part of the model of programming that I have, as well as an entire system for the implementation of those fatigue singles. A big part of fatigue singles, though, is the entirety of my system of programming, which this video is very much a spin-off of what I'm doing over on Powerlifting now over the next five months, so if there's some... Things I'm going to go through in this video, then I'm not going to fully describe, that aren't going to make complete sense unless you watch those videos. This month is the first month of that five-part series, which is the video on block periodization's updated approach. Next month is going to be creating predictability in a dynamic RPE system, and then the three months after that will be a whole three-part series on peaking. All of these videos build upon each other, and this is kind of a spin-off of having an understanding of, ‘Okay, so within this model and system of an updated approach to block periodization, block periodization and creating predictability in dynamic RPE systems, how am I going to implement it?’ Singles allow us to create as little disruption as possible. The other caveat I'll mention is that I have a whole video on programming singles that's almost an hour long, so there are a lot of topics that I'm not going to cover in this video, such as who should do singles, who should not do singles, and why you would do singles. There are many different things that I cover in that video that I won't discuss here. I'm really just going to dive into the implementation and the reasoning behind fatigue singles, and why this has become a staple within my model of programming. So, wrapping back around to the videos I'm doing on powerlifting now, I can provide a very, very, very baseline summary of those: we are trying to... The program aims to create as little disruption block to block as possible and not make big changes, but instead make micro changes. One of the issues with singles is that a lot of times, when people implement them and haven't been using them prior, it causes a pretty large disruption to the program as a whole. This contrasts with a system where the model is built around doing singles, such as the flex training systems model or conjugate systems—those systems that use singles year-round and all the time. The staple of the system is doing those singles consistently and having everything built around those. However, if it's not built around those singles and we implement them, there are a lot of things that can go wrong when we do so. So, what do I... What I mean by singles can be fairly disruptive because let's be honest, in the grand scheme of things, unless you're Bob, Ashton, or Jesus, someone lifting an enormous amount of weight, a single in powerlifting is, frankly, one of the easiest things you can do, barring you're completely maxing out. But let's say a single at a seven or eight; it's a very low stress and low fatigue movement. The issue is that people, when they do singles way too often, mistake fatigue for actually being more of an adrenaline jump, adrenaline dump, or over-prioritization. So that's something I talk about a lot in my full video encompassing singles, which is where people go wrong with singles. The main one I'm going to kind of talk about here is the fact that when... Someone does a single first; they typically put way too much priority on it. They put way too much adrenaline, focus, and motivation. They get too amped up for it, and they tend to get a big dump afterwards. The work after suffers because of that. To the lifter, they say, "Oh, I'm just really fatigued after the single." But the fact of the matter is, when you implement a fatigued single style system, where they do the single after the rep set, you'll find that all of a sudden, magically, all of their lifts, the totality of the workout, tend to improve. It's the same reasoning for ascending sets. A lot of people will do ascending sets because if they use it as a top rep set and then back off, they'll see a big adrenaline dump on those back. Offsets versus if they do ascending sets, they'll see their quality of work in average intensity increase. It's the same thought process with fatigue singles. So in summary, the reason to do a fatigue single, or a single after the top rep set, is to create as little disruption as possible, improve the quality of the work, and the totality of the workout, and improve the metrics of average intensity and total tonnage across week to week and block to block. That you're going to be accumulating by having better overall work. And to that, you might say, is there really that much of a difference? To me, at first, when I used to do these more sparingly, I would have said probably no, but the more I do these, I've seen a pretty dramatic.

The difference, and that's where we're going to now get into our case studies and eventually get into some application of how to program and program these over a macro cycle. But we're going to take a look at Waskar in his prep leading to the Power of the American Nationals, where we were implementing fatigue singles. We pulled away from those and started prioritizing the top single but saw some issues that we ran into. When I started kind of looking at the data, I saw some pretty profound differences in what happened and why we saw a drop-off in strength in that final block leading into the meet. So, getting into Waskar's meet prep, we're going to look at the three blocks that led into his Power of the American Nationals competition. I'm convincing some of this. One, we're only going to look at the main squat day. I'm also condensing this to make it very simple to kind of look at. There's a little bit more to it than this, but this still gives the general gist of things. So, if we're looking at block one, we had fatigue singles. We had his top set of four, followed by a single, followed by four back offsets. One thing to note here, and I'll mention a little bit about something we did different later on, is his back offset was a percentage drop from that top rep set. So, whatever we did on that top rep set, then we calculated what to do on his back offset. That's very important as we get through this. So, we can see here, as he went through this first block, we were... Prioritizing that rep work, he eventually ended the final week with, I believe, a PR set of four at 212.5. Even after that, he hit a single at 222.5, which was 9 to 10 RPE. It was very, very tough, but either way, the quality of the work on this day was fantastic, and 222.5 was at least the body weight he was at a current PR. One thing to notate here that kind of preceded all this was that he eventually hit 217.5 in the meat; he probably could have hit 220. We're going to get to kind of what happened towards the end of prep that led to this drop-off that we're seeing. So, in the fatigue single block, we see very good rep work performance, and we still see a pretty good singles performance. Two blocks out, we started prioritizing singles, and overall this. The block went really, really well. You can see here we worked our way up; he's hitting some great singles, and he finishes with a PR single at 227 and a half, or 227.5. Fantastic! We were on cloud nine, and everything was looking like he was going to hit a massive PR come meet time. But one thing to notice here, before we get into the next block, is notice the rep work he's now doing: a top set of three, yet he's doing seven and a half kilos less; top set of three, five kilos less; top set of three, seven and a half kilos less; top set of three, seven and a half kilos less. And then, again, a mistake on my part as a coach, because it's all percentage-based off of that rep set. All of his back offsets are lower too; I mean, he's doing weights for a triple on his back offs that... They are five kilos lower than he's doing for a four by four. There are issues here; we didn't see them on this block because we were still able to carry on and hold the adaptations from this block. However, in the block after this, we started to see some issues arise from this big drop in average intensity. In the report, we get into that final peaking block, and we're continuing to prioritize singles. We have a good idea that he is cutting weight, so we figured that maybe this is going to drop off a little bit; but unfortunately, it drops off a good deal. You can see here he eventually hits 220 at what was like a 9 to 10 RPE. Considering he hit 222.5 after a rep set on block one and then 227.5, this is a little disappointing. It wasn't bad, but it was. Definitely a big downturn. Again, we can look at this: now he's hitting a double at 210, which is two and a half kilos less than needed for a set of four. He did a double at 200, five kilos less, and a double at 195, two and a half kilos less. He did a double at 185, five kilos less than this four. Once we started implementing these singles, his rep work took a big hit, and that could be partially because the athlete needs to have a little bit of a better understanding that they need to make sure to continue to push and prioritize that rep work. But that's probably more on me as a coach. Things I learned eventually that I'm going to talk about—I'll talk about it now—is eventually I did percentage-based back-off work, so that was set and not calculating off. Of those hop rep sets, we wanted to keep that more standardized so that the average intensity didn't drop too much, even if we saw some of the rep work kind of fluctuating based off of singles. But the biggest thing we're going to get to is that we just decided to implement fatigue singles for a longer period of time. Because while this simple little thing of doing one set before the other doesn't seem like a big deal, let's look at what happened here. My math might not be perfect; I'm not a statistician, but I think this will give a good idea and overall, it will be able to kind of replicate what I'm trying to talk about here.

So, looking at this first block, arguably this first block was maybe the most productive. Block one and block two both went really well, but if I’m looking at the totality of the workload done, this first block was really, really good. If we're looking at that top rep set, we had an average. I'm using the fact that if you look here at the calculations, I'm using 227.5 as his max. I’m using that to kind of calculate average intensity since he hit this as his 1RM, and that was his best rep of the entire prep. 227.5 is his top end, so I’m using that. So his average intensity of his top rep set was 88.46. If I’m taking all four top rep sets, I’m taking the single he was at 92.86, and if we’re taking the back offsets, the four-by-fours, he was on average 78.85 for a total average, which this isn't perfect because obviously it’s... It's disproportionate that he only did one rep here and he did four reps here. He needed a four by four here; this isn't perfect. I'm literally just calculating the fact that these are all equal. It still kind of gets to the point, but here, 86.72 is the average intensity if we're just looking at these three calculations as well as the total tonnage. When we get into the next block, we'll see that the top single average intensity goes up. Well, it should have; we were pushing it a bit harder. Initially, it goes from 92.86 to 95.05, so you can see here a 2.2 percent increase, which is good but not drastic. I mean, all we did was hit five kilos more in the grand scheme of things; that's a difference by putting it. First, but it's not a massive difference in comparison to the fact that we took a big hit on the report. Now, we're only doing our average intensity on the top set of three, which was 85.4 percent. Yeah, it's only a three percent drop from this, but we have to factor in he was doing one rep less. So, once we factor that in, if I do a three percent addition—because, in general, if you've watched my videos before, one rep is about three percent—that was a six percent drop in average intensity of his rep set. Even though the reps were dropping and he should be going heavier, he did seven and a half kilos less with a rep less. That's disheartening. Then, the fact is that I also calculated all of his back-off work, which I didn't do all the calculations for. Here, but you can obviously see, it basically equates four by four and then one by three to three by five. Pretty similar; they shouldn't be drastically different. But you can see here the average back offset is 78.85. Even the triple here, if we're just doing the average intensity of that triple, it's 76.92. Average intensity dropped, and then volume dropped, which shouldn't have happened because, in the grand scheme of things, we were doing pretty similar volume. If you equate one by four to four by four, and so two by three and three by five, it equates. I actually think this is one total rep more. Yeah, that should be one total rep more. Incense, and that doesn't mean always volume is going to be higher, but they should be basically equated volume-wise. But we ended up doing 2.4, 2.46 percent less total tonnage, not because we changed the actual repetition schemes too much, but because of the intensity drop causing a two percent drop. So, not only do we have a six percent drop in average intensity on the report, we also had a 2.4 drop in total tonnage on the volume. Then we get to that final block where we start to see that downturn. Now, the average intensity, even though we're trying to push the heaviest lifts of prep and we're prioritizing, is actually lower than what we did on that first block when that single was masked or fatigued behind that top set of four. So, even though we're doing a double instead of a top set of four, we still had an average intensity drop. We're actually doing less weight than he was when he was doing sets of four. So, not only was it about a 1.5 percent drop just from straight weight, but adding the fact that the rep changes, it's now about a 4.65 intensity drop, and that's affecting the back-off work. Again, now we're doing fours; we're doing fours again, so it's a four by four. Earlier in the block, it was a one by two and a three by four, but we adjusted that. Either way, it's pretty similar. If you're looking at this, he's doing a four by four at 177.5 versus a four by four at 190 because of the difference in how it was calculated. So, there's a 12.5-kilo difference in the back offsets because of how this all played out. And then, to add on top of that, a really big... Drop in total tonnage. Now, I was expecting that because we were dropping reps here to an extent, but the fact of the matter is, especially once we got to weeks three and four, as I started adding some volume back in, it was only a two-rep drop. Instead of doing a double or a set of four, you're just doing a double, so it's only a two-rep drop change. However, we eventually saw a total drop in the average weekly tonnage over those four weeks of 19.27, mainly due to the slight changes in the rep schemes of the doubles, but even more so in the changes in just the average intensity.

This is where it became incredibly apparent to me, and I saw this not only with Waskar, which is a bit more extreme of an example, but I saw this with many athletes across the board. The boards across the board, so I started kind of deciding I'm going to start implementing this system, which I was already doing to an extent for the most part. That is going to prioritize this single, staying behind the top rep set for as long as possible. So how does that play out? I'm going to give you some options here for program design. Within this program design, this is going to make a lot more sense if you were to watch the powerlifting Now videos. I'm going to run through this pretty quickly because I'm not going to describe all the things I talk about there. But here we have a three-block setup that would be pretty similar to what I'm using as a template for what we might do. So, in the first block, we're doing a top... Set of five followed by back-off fives in the single. Block two: set of four followed by back-off fours. Block three: top set of three followed by four by five. There are ways we can do this fatigue drop, so with the assumption that we're using RPEs on that top set, it's going to stay relatively static block to block. Again, powerlifting. Now, I explain that a lot more, but what we can do to maintain this average intensity and this tonnage that was affected by us prioritizing that single and how it affected the rep work is, one, like I said, obviously what I need to do. I mentioned here, you can either do a percent drop from the top set or percentage-based. We are doing percentage-based moving forward. Here, but even so, we have a three-block progression of a very slow adjustment and change, prioritizing those singles slowly. So, no matter what, we are continuing to implement the fatigue single system where it’s afterwards. In this first block, we’re very much prioritizing the rep set; that’s first. It’s a higher RPE, and we’re prioritizing it. You can see here the singles are very much what we’ll call skill practice, around six RPE to seven RPE. They are there; we’re looking to improve them throughout the block, but they are very much a low priority in comparison to the top set of five, even though they are of intense intensity. You’re probably going—you’re not probably; you’re going to do more on this single than you are doing on. That set of five is an increased intensity on the absolute end, as we kind of build up from that set of five. What that does for a lifter is, because it's more weight, it tends to be motivating. Anytime a lifter gets to go up in weight, there tends to be a novelty to that versus dropping down in weight, which is one of the issues of doing the single and then dropping down to a set of five. So here, we can see that first block has a high priority on rep work singles. Take a Big Mac C block two; we continue to prioritize that rep work at the top set of four. You can see the same exact RPE progression, but we're going to start to build on that single a bit more and build up to a little bit of a heavier weight to an 8 RPE, very much what you kind of saw with. Wascar's first block that we did here, even though this got pushed a little bit more, which is completely fine. Then after that, we'll call it like a peaking block, per se. What we can do is, in Wascar's case, where we saw a pretty profound difference, we're going to continue to prioritize that top set of three. But since the RPE on the single is going to start to build up a bit more, instead of doing a five to a six and building up to like an eight to nine by block four, we're going to do a five, six, seven, eight ascending model of RPE there on the rep work, while we do a six, seven, eight, nine on the single. So the average intensity should work itself out because of that. But here, this is where we're going to see ourselves be able to continue to work in. The fatigued single system prioritizes the rep work. We don't create too much disruption, but at the right time, we are able to prioritize that single to see what that top-end strength is come meet time. So, in this peaking block, they're still doing that top triple first, lower RPE, so we should have a little bit more energy for that single. We're going to start to build on that single, and then in the final week, before maybe we taper—or maybe this is the final week of a regular block or a macro cycle—we want to kind of test and push more towards hitting a new PR. We put that single first, then shift that triple to second, followed by the back-off work. Another option, because again, this depends on the lifter: how disproportioned are they when... They do fatigued singles versus doing the single first.

Are they as extreme as Wascar, or is it more of a slight difference? So another option for option two is, you can have that same first block. On the second block, you will have that single be first to have a little bit more of a test, to let that be a bit more pronounced, followed by that top set of four. Then, on that third block, again you have all the same models. Option one, you build up with the rep work, and then, week four, you have that single be the first option before doing that top triple. Again, mainly on both of these blocks, just to have the skill practice of being able to do those first unfatigued, to be able to kind of express full strength. And the last option, which is... What I think a lot of people can do, it just depends on what is best for you. Again, the first block is the same: prioritize the rep work. In the second block, you can either prioritize the rep work or have the single first, and then in the final block, lead into the meet. That's when you finally prioritize a single. Honestly, with Wasco, we could have done that. You can see here, this block went great, and then the second block continued to go really well because we were able to carry over these adaptations. He hadn't detrained off of this rep work yet, so he was able to express this top-end strength for Wasco. We very well could use this option three, where we make sure to prioritize the single or the rep work. Blocks one and two suppress the single as a fatigue single afterwards, and then finally the final block, whether again it's either meat prep and this is the block leading into the meet, or this is just something we're using at the end of a macro cycle to kind of test or push singles. We prioritize that single for the final block before then shifting back into the beginning of the macro cycle again and working to prioritize in that rep work. So that summarizes the implementation within my system and the model of how I'm using fatigue singles when we're looking at a macro cycle view, whether that's just a regular training block or a peaking block into a meet. Again, this makes a lot more sense within the totality of the system that I'm. Talking about powerlifting now, with all five videos I'm doing, so definitely make sure to check that out. But hopefully, even within that, you can still get a good idea of how you can use this within your own coaching, or within your own self-coaching, or lifters. Anything that can help you as a powerlifter to improve your training, and how you can be able to use singles and not disrupt your training too much from what its normal flow is and what works best for you. And as always, if you have any questions, make sure to comment down below. Make sure to like the video, share it with those who you think may benefit from it, and make sure you're subscribed if you're not already. Until next time, peace..
